name: Wei Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying business at Kingsford University, and I live above my family's noodle restaurant, Golden Bowl, on Mill Street. Lectures are Monday to Thursday, and then I'm in the kitchen or at the till from five until close, and all day Saturday. On Sundays we go to the community temple, then I do my reading. It's a full week, but I'm used to full weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do your parents expect from your degree?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My parents opened the restaurant fifteen years ago, and my grandmother still makes the broth. They don't pay me properly, I get pocket money and meals, and loans pay for my fees. Under a month of savings, if I'm honest. I'm the first to go to university. I don't use AI tools, and I don't see why I should, because the restaurant runs on hands and trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one's called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. People talk a lot, and then life goes on. The restaurant still needs cooks and someone to carry the bowls, and no program does that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even in that case, I'm worried. Rents on Mill Street have gone up, and customers are fewer since the office near us closed. If the restaurant has a bad year, my parents will need me to work more, and that cuts into my studies. Loans are growing too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: lectures, the evening shift, the temple on Sundays. I'd learn the restaurant's accounts from my father, so I can take them over one day. I'd try to find a business placement where I can work with a small firm. I wouldn't change the way I study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but a little heavy. I carry the family's hopes, and I don't want to let them down. I'd say it's like carrying a full tray through a crowded room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your parents depend on the restaurant. What happens to your plans if the restaurant has a bad year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my own costs first, like skipping the class trip and the bus pass. Then I'd work extra evenings. My parents would never ask, but I'd offer. It's my duty, and I wouldn't resent it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel any pull to start using the AI tools your classmates talk about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Classmates say it writes essays, and I think that's cheating yourself. I'd rather learn slowly and know it than copy fast and not understand. My grandmother says a shortcut in the kitchen shows in the bowl.

say: I'd say it's what I expected: people talk a lot and **life goes on**.
The restaurant still needs **cooks** and someone to carry the bowls.
think: Rents on Mill Street have risen and **customers** are fewer since the nearby office closed.
A bad year means my parents need me to **work more**, which cuts into study.
do: Keep up lectures, the evening shift and the **temple** on Sundays.
Learn the restaurant's **accounts** from my father.
Look for a **business placement** with a small firm.
feel: Steady but **heavy**, like carrying a full tray through a crowded room.
S0.quote: I carry the family's hopes, and I don't want to let them down. I'd say it's like carrying a full tray through a crowded room.
fieldNote: His worry is **the restaurant's money**, not AI itself.
Family duty and loyalty shape every choice.
He rejects AI tools on moral grounds, calling it cheating yourself.

steps.text: Keep working the evening shift at Golden Bowl
Skip the class trip and the bus pass to cut costs
Learn the restaurant's accounts from my father

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one's called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should keep our heads down and work. Some tasks will change, but people still want food made by hands. I'd keep it simple, and not follow every trend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one worries me more than the others. Business is booking, planning, buying and checking, which the card says go first. If the jobs at the end of my degree shrink, then my parents' sacrifice means less. I'd be slow to learn the tools, so I'd be behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying and tighten the restaurant's side. I'd take over the ordering and bookings from my mother, so I understand each part. I'd ask my business lecturer which firms still hire people and which jobs are mostly human. And I might try one tool, if my cousin sits with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It feels like a storm far off. You don't see it yet, but you can smell it. I'd keep working and trying not to show it at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of those thinking tasks would a restaurant use first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering, bookings and customer replies. Delivery apps already do some of it for us. If a machine took bookings and ordered supplies, my mother would have an hour back, which would be a good thing, but then who needs me?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your classmates start getting jobs with these tools and you haven't, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to learn, slowly. I'd take a short course. It would be uncomfortable, but pride is no use when the rent is due. I'd also remind myself that I know people and trust, which counts for a lot in business.

say: I'd say we should **keep our heads down** and work, because people still want food made by hands.
think: Business is booking, planning and buying, which go first, so my **degree** may count for less.
I'd be slow to learn the tools, so I'd be **behind**.
do: Take over the **ordering** and bookings from my mother to learn each part.
Ask my business lecturer which jobs remain **mostly human**.
Try **one tool** if my cousin sits with me.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a storm far off: you can smell it but not see it.
S1.quote: Pride is no use when the rent is due. I'd also remind myself that I know people and trust, which counts for a lot in business.
fieldNote: He sees **pride** as something to put aside when needed.
Relies on relationships and trust as his edge.
Needs a trusted person, his cousin, to start with the tools.

steps.text: Take over ordering and bookings at Golden Bowl from Mum
Try one AI tool with my cousin sitting beside me
Take a short course on running a small business
Keep the evening shifts and Saturday work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one's called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should stay calm and look after our own. In two years people can't solve everything. I'd tell my friends at the temple to check on their elders and neighbours, and look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think my degree might never pay off. If thinking work goes in two years, what's a business degree for? My parents spent years saving, and I'd have debt for it. I'd feel I let them down, even though it wouldn't be my fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my parents and ask for an honest talk about money. I'd consider leaving university for a year and working full-time at the restaurant, because that work is hands-on and lasts longer. Or I might do an apprenticeship in catering management. I'd keep the temple and our community close, since they would be our support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and ashamed. I don't like saying it. I'd feel I should have seen it coming. But I'd also feel closer to my family, because we'd all be in it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. Who in the family do you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandmother. She's old and the work is hard on her. I'd want her not to carry the broth pots on her own. I'd hire a helper if I could, or do the heavy parts myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your parents to do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to tell me the real numbers. They hide the bad months from me. If I knew exactly how my parents' restaurant is doing, I could plan properly and help.

say: I'd say stay **calm** and look after our own, and tell friends at the temple to check on their elders.
People can't solve everything in two years.
think: My degree might **never pay off**: what's a business degree for if thinking work goes?
I'd feel I **let my parents down**, though it wouldn't be my fault.
do: Ask my parents for an honest talk about **money**.
Consider a **year out** working full-time at the restaurant.
Look at an **apprenticeship** in catering management.
feel: **Frightened and ashamed**, but closer to my family.
S2.quote: If I knew exactly how my parents' restaurant is doing, I could plan properly and help.
fieldNote: Shame and **family duty** drive his reaction more than money.
Would put the degree on hold in order to stay close to home.
Wants honesty at home, which his parents currently avoid.

steps.text: Ask my parents for an honest talk about the restaurant's money
Consider a year out working full-time at Golden Bowl
Lean on the temple community for support and advice
Stop adding to my loan until the plan is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one's called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to be sensible. We'd need to look after the older people first, and keep families together. I'd say what I think at the temple and keep it simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's easier to bear. I'd graduate and maybe start working at the restaurant properly before it hits. I'd still be worried, but five years feels like time to prepare, and I like to prepare. I'd be able to make my parents proud before things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and use the placement to learn how to run a small business properly. I'd teach myself a bit of bookkeeping software, just the basics. I'd save in a separate account every summer, and make sure the restaurant has an emergency fund. I'd keep going to the temple, because it keeps me grounded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but I'd still be a bit tight in the chest. I'd keep to routine, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years puts you at graduation in 2029. What changes compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the restaurant stays a place where the regulars sit and talk. Even if machines do more of the cooking one day, people still want a place that feels like home. I'd like to keep it, and maybe open a second small one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your hope for the restaurant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's panic. With five there's a plan, and a plan is something I can hold on to.

say: I'd say five years gives us time to be **sensible**, looking after older people first.
I'd say what I think at the temple and keep it simple.
think: I'd **graduate** and could work at the restaurant properly before it hits.
Five years feels like time to **prepare**, and I like to prepare.
do: Use my placement to learn how to run a **small business**.
Teach myself **bookkeeping** software, just the basics.
Save in a **separate account** each summer for an emergency fund.
feel: **Calmer**, but still a bit tight in the chest, so I keep to routine.
S3.quote: With two years there's panic. With five there's a plan, and a plan is something I can hold on to.
fieldNote: Time lets him turn **duty into a plan**, which is how he copes.
Learns one practical tool, bookkeeping software, on his own terms.
Hopes for a second restaurant, a traditional business ambition.

steps.text: Learn basic bookkeeping software for the restaurant
Open a separate emergency fund for the restaurant
Use my placement to learn small business management
Keep the temple routine and the evening shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one's called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to use well. People should be training, saving and looking after their families. I wouldn't expect the government to fix it, but I'd want it to help those who can't help themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be twenty-eight, probably running the restaurant with my parents' guidance, and maybe married. I'd feel quite settled. Ten years is long enough that I'd see the changes coming, and my business would be ready for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and work for a firm for two or three years to learn properly. Then I'd return to the restaurant, bring in simple tools for booking and ordering, and keep the cooking and the welcome human. I'd keep an emergency fund and look after my grandmother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It's the first one where I can picture a normal life. I'd still work hard, but I wouldn't be afraid every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what do you want to have done by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I'd like a business degree used well, a restaurant that's still ours, and maybe a family of my own. I'd want my parents to retire without worry. That's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk in feeling safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If I felt too safe, I'd stop learning. I'd keep asking what could go wrong and talk to people outside the community, so I don't miss things. Being careful is a habit that keeps a business alive.

say: I'd say ten years is time to use well: **train, save** and look after our families.
I'd want government help for those who can't help themselves.
think: By twenty-eight I'd be **running the restaurant** with my parents' guidance, quite settled.
Ten years is long enough to see the changes **coming**.
do: Finish the degree and work for a **firm** for two or three years.
Return to the restaurant and bring in simple tools for **booking and ordering**.
Keep an **emergency fund** and look after my grandmother.
feel: Fairly **calm**: the first scenario where I can picture a normal life.
S4.quote: If I felt too safe, I'd stop learning. I'd keep asking what could go wrong and talk to people outside the community, so I don't miss things.
fieldNote: Ten years gives him a **normal life** to picture, with the family restaurant at the centre.
He plans to bring in simple tools only for booking and ordering.
Says safety can make him lazy, a sign of caution.

steps.text: Work two or three years at a firm to learn properly
Bring a simple booking and ordering system into Golden Bowl
Build an emergency fund for the restaurant
Help my parents retire without worry

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time, and my parents' years of saving would be tied to a degree that might not pay. What would help is honest advice, a way to pause the loans and community support. Also my parents telling me the restaurant's real numbers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against change. I'm slow to it. If someone I trust shows me a tool and why it matters, I'll try it. A stranger telling me to adapt just makes me dig in.

headlineQuote: A shortcut in the kitchen shows in the bowl.
portrait: Wei is an **18-year-old** business student who lives above his family's noodle restaurant and works there most evenings.
He avoids **AI tools**, trusts family, faith and community, and measures worth by hard work.
He is **anxious** in the first scenarios and alarmed at two years, with shame about letting his parents down.
With ten years he is **calm** and pictures running the restaurant with simple tools.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario: his degree might not pay off after his parents' years of saving.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest advice**, a way to pause loans, community support and his parents sharing the restaurant's real numbers.
